claims.text: High-temperature exposure in an oxidizing atmosphere causes the high-entropy alloy to form an oxide layer.
The oxide layer formed by the high-entropy alloy is stable.
The protective oxide layer grows slowly.
Synergistic interactions among multiple principal elements govern oxide-layer formation.
Synergistic interactions among multiple principal elements improve oxide-layer adhesion.
Formation of a stable, slow-growing oxide layer enhances oxidation resistance.
The high-entropy alloy will retain its protective oxide layer during high-temperature oxidation.
The high-entropy alloy will have superior oxidation resistance to conventional Ni-based or Co-based alloys under the same conditions.
Relative to conventional alloys, the high-entropy alloy is expected to exhibit a slower oxidation rate.
Relative to conventional alloys, the high-entropy alloy is expected to form a thinner oxide layer.
Relative to conventional alloys, the high-entropy alloy is expected to exhibit improved oxide-layer adhesion.
The proposed hypothesis applies between 800°C and 1200°C.
The proposed hypothesis applies in air or oxygen.
The proposed hypothesis applies to near-equiatomic alloys containing five or more principal elements.
The exact roles of individual alloying elements and their interactions in oxide-layer formation and stability are not well understood.

contradictions.description: The conditions specify temperatures above 800°C, whereas the boundary includes 800°C as the lower endpoint.
